findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher never actually validates the grant-type shortcut
findings.body: In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the grant shortcut is supposed to occupy characters at index 4-5 of the 6-char context prefix (2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type), but the code extracts `items[0].substring(3, 5)` instead of `substring(4, 6)`, picking the wrong characters. On top of that, the boolean logic is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (no match) when the (wrong) substring equals the expected shortcut, and otherwise falls through to only check the UUID portion. Combining the wrong substring with the inverted condition means the comparison practically never triggers a failure based on the expected grant shortcut — the matcher effectively validates only the UUID suffix and silently ignores the grant-type encoding it claims to check. All the `expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` assertions that rely on `isAccessTokenId(...)` therefore do not actually verify that the correct grant-type shortcut was encoded into the access token id, defeating the purpose of this test helper and of the related integration tests.

findings.title: Constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId for null
findings.body: In the `AccessTokenContext` constructor, `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed")` is called twice (lines 72 and 73); the second call reuses `grantType` instead of `rawTokenId`, despite the message claiming to check `rawTokenId`. As a result, a null `rawTokenId` is never actually rejected. If `rawTokenId` is ever null (e.g., due to a caller bug), it will silently flow into `encodeTokenId()` and produce a malformed token id (`...:null`) instead of failing fast with a clear error.

findings.title: Access token id format changed from plain UUID to a prefixed, colon-delimited string
findings.body: `initToken()` previously set the token id (`jti`) to a plain UUID via `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()`. Now the id is produced by `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)`, which prepends a 6-character context prefix and a colon (e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...`) before the UUID. This is a visible change to the structure/length of the standard `jti` claim for every access token issued going forward. Any external system, client library, logging/SIEM tooling, or custom Keycloak extension that parses or validates the access token id as a bare UUID (length 36, dash positions, etc.) will break. The PR does not appear to document this as a breaking change or provide an opt-out/compatibility mode for consumers relying on the previous format.

findings.title: Removal of public copy constructor breaks binary/source compatibility for OAuth2GrantType.Context
findings.body: The previously public `Context(Context context)` copy constructor has been removed entirely from `OAuth2GrantType.Context`, which lives in `server-spi-private` and is part of the SPI surface used by custom/extension `OAuth2GrantType` implementations. Any third-party code (or future in-tree code) that relied on this copy constructor to clone/extend a `Context` instance will fail to compile after this change. Since this is an SPI-facing class, its public constructors should be treated as part of the public contract and removing one without deprecation is a breaking API change.

findings.title: Non-atomic two-map update when lazily resolving unknown grant shortcuts
findings.body: `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` update the two `ConcurrentHashMap`s (`grantsByShortcuts` and `grantsToShortcuts`) with separate, non-atomic `put` calls when a grant type is not found in the initially populated maps (e.g., a provider deployed after `postInit`). Under concurrent requests triggering the same lazy-resolution path, one thread could observe one map updated but not the other, leading to a transient inconsistency between the two maps. While the code recovers on subsequent calls, this is a minor race that could be avoided by computing both updates together (e.g., with `computeIfAbsent` or a lock) rather than as two sequential, independently-visible writes.
